paragraphs: A file is a collection of related data stored on a secondary storage device.

blocks.text: Files preserve data beyond one program execution. A C program opens a stream, reads or writes through it, and closes it. <stdio.h> declares the file-handling functions and FILE type.

paragraphs: Text files represent data as characters; binary files store data in a chosen byte representation.

rows: Numbers are formatted as readable characters, such as "123".
An int can be written as its native object bytes using fwrite.
Open using r, w or a (and optional +).
Add b, for example rb or wb.
Text-mode translation, such as newline conversion, may occur.
Binary mode avoids text-mode translation.
Use fprintf/fscanf, fgets/fputs, fgetc/fputc.
Use fread/fwrite for blocks.
Readable with a suitable text editor and encoding.
Reading requires knowledge of the representation.

blocks.text: Both occupy bytes physically. Native binary object files can depend on machine representation; they are not automatically portable or smaller. EOF is a library status value, not a mandatory character stored at the end of a file.

paragraphs: Sequential access processes data in order; random access repositions the stream before reading or writing.

rows: Read the next item from the current position.
Seek to a permitted position using fseek, then read/write.
Suitable for processing every record in order.
Suitable for direct access to fixed-size records.
Example: loop over all integers with fscanf.
Example: fseek(fp, 2L * record_size, SEEK_SET) selects the third fixed-size binary record.

blocks.text: These are access methods, rather than incompatible physical file types. Seeking requires a stream that supports positioning.

paragraphs: A file pointer is a pointer of type FILE * used to identify and manage an open stream.

blocks.code:
FILE *fp = fopen("data.txt", "r");
if (fp == NULL) { /* opening failed */ }

blocks.text: Pass fp to functions such as fgetc, fprintf and fclose. The FILE object maintains stream state, including buffering and position; fp is not a pointer directly to the current character in the disk file. Do not use a stream after fclose.

paragraphs: The mode argument of fopen controls permitted operations and creation/truncation.

rows: r
Read an existing file; fails if absent.
w
Write; create or truncate to empty.
a
Append; create if absent. Writes go to the end.
r+
Read and write an existing file; no initial truncation.
w+
Read and write; create or truncate.
a+
Read and append; create if absent. Every write goes to the end.

blocks.text: Add b for binary mode, as in rb, wb or r+b. With update streams (+), switching between reading and writing requires the appropriate positioning/flush operation: output followed by input needs fflush or positioning; input followed by output needs positioning unless the input reached EOF.

paragraphs: fseek changes the file-position indicator of a stream.

blocks.code: int fseek(FILE *stream, long offset, int origin);

blocks.text: stream identifies the open file. offset is the displacement. origin is SEEK_SET (beginning), SEEK_CUR (current position) or SEEK_END (end). It returns 0 on success and nonzero on failure.
For portable text-stream use, an offset is zero or a position previously returned by ftell with SEEK_SET.

paragraphs: These statements change the position of a suitable seekable binary stream.

blocks.code: fseek(fptr, 15L, SEEK_SET);

blocks.text: Move to offset 15 bytes from the beginning: the next byte is the 16th byte, counting the first byte as position 0.

blocks.code: fseek(fptr, -5L, SEEK_END);

blocks.text: Move five bytes before the end. In a 20-byte file, this is also offset 15. The file must support this seek and be long enough.
Check the return value (0 means success). These arbitrary byte offsets are not portable text-stream positioning; some streams do not support SEEK_END.

paragraphs: fread and fwrite transfer blocks of data.

blocks.code:
size_t fread(void *ptr, size_t size, size_t count, FILE *stream);
size_t fwrite(const void *ptr, size_t size, size_t count, FILE *stream);

blocks.text: ptr addresses the objects, size is bytes per object, count is the requested number of objects, and stream is the open stream. The return value is the number of complete objects transferred, not necessarily the number of bytes. Check it against count; inspect ferror after a short read to distinguish an error from EOF.

paragraphs: Use return values and stream indicators to detect file errors.

items.text: fopen: NULL means opening failed.
ferror(fp): nonzero means the stream error indicator is set.
feof(fp): nonzero means a read has encountered end-of-file.
clearerr(fp): clears both error and EOF indicators.
perror("context"): prints context and the message associated with errno; use after a failing operation that supplies errno.
fclose(fp): EOF indicates closing/flushing failed.

blocks.text: Drive input loops by the read result, not while(!feof(fp)). End-of-file is detected after an attempted read, and is not itself a read error.

paragraphs: Preprocessor directives prepare the source before it is compiled.

blocks.text: 1. File inclusion

blocks.code:
#include <stdio.h>
#include "student.h"

blocks.text: Angle brackets request an implementation-provided header; quotes first use the implementation’s quoted-header search. Headers provide declarations and macros, rather than linking library implementations.
2. Macro substitution

blocks.code:
#define PI 3.14
#define SQR(x) ((x) * (x))
#undef SQR

blocks.text: An object-like macro replaces a name with tokens. A function-like macro substitutes its arguments. Parentheses preserve operator grouping; repeated argument evaluation still requires care.
3. Conditional compilation

Conditional directives select which source is compiled. #ifdef tests whether a macro is defined; #ifndef tests the opposite. #error produces a diagnostic, #line changes presumed line/file information, and #pragma requests implementation-specific behavior.

paragraphs: Use return values and stream indicators to detect file errors.

items.text: fopen: NULL means opening failed.
ferror(fp): nonzero means the stream error indicator is set.
feof(fp): nonzero means a read has encountered end-of-file.
clearerr(fp): clears both error and EOF indicators.
perror("context"): prints context and the message associated with errno; use after a failing operation that supplies errno.
fclose(fp): EOF indicates closing/flushing failed.

blocks.text: Drive input loops by the read result, not while(!feof(fp)). End-of-file is detected after an attempted read, and is not itself a read error.

Normal completion sets the EOF indicator, not the error indicator. clearerr resets the indicators but does not move the file position. A missing input pathname exercises the NULL check without using an invalid FILE pointer.

paragraphs: Random access changes the stream position so that data can be accessed without reading every preceding item.

rows: fseek
int fseek(FILE *fp, long offset, int origin); returns 0 on successful positioning.
ftell
long ftell(FILE *fp); returns the position, or -1L on failure.
rewind
void rewind(FILE *fp); moves to the start and clears EOF and error indicators.

blocks.text: SEEK_SET uses the beginning, SEEK_CUR the current position, and SEEK_END the end. For a seekable binary stream, offsets count bytes where supported. For a text stream, use offset 0 or an ftell-derived position with SEEK_SET; ftell is not a portable text-file-size calculation.
P is the 16th letter and lies at offset 15. In a 20-byte file, five before the end reaches that same byte. rewind returns to A. fseek clears EOF on success; rewind also clears the error indicator.

paragraphs: enum declares an enumeration type and named integer constants; #define creates a preprocessor macro.

rows: Parsed by the compiler as a C declaration.
Replaced as tokens before compilation.
Enumerators are integer constant expressions (type int in C11).
Replacement can be a number, string or expression.
Enumeration constants obey C identifier scope.
Macro definitions last until #undef or the end of preprocessing; braces do not establish macro scope.

blocks.text: Use enum for a related set of integer choices. A macro can represent more general replacements. C enumerations are not strongly type-safe enums as in some other languages.

paragraphs: typedef introduces a type alias; #define performs token substitution.

rows: Understood by the compiler and obeys C scope rules.
Processed before compilation; not constrained by C block scope.
Can name types, not arbitrary expression replacements.
Can replace types, values or token sequences.
Example: typedef unsigned int Count;
Example: #define LIMIT 100

blocks.code:
typedef int *IntPtr;
IntPtr a, b;       /* both pointers */
#define INT_PTR int *
INT_PTR c, d;      /* c is a pointer, d is int */

blocks.text: The macro expands textually to int *c, d. The typedef alias applies the complete pointer type to both declarators. Prefer a typedef when a true type alias is intended.

paragraphs: File-handling functions open, transfer data, position and close streams.

rows: Open
fopen(filename, mode): FILE* on success, NULL on failure.
Character I/O
fgetc(fp) reads an int or EOF; fputc(ch, fp) writes one character.
Line I/O
fgets(buffer, size, fp) reads a bounded line; fputs(text, fp) writes a string.
Formatted I/O
fprintf(fp, format, ...) writes values; fscanf(fp, format, ...) converts input.
Block I/O
fread(ptr, size, count, fp) and fwrite transfer complete objects.
Position
fseek changes position; ftell reports it; rewind returns to the start.
Status
feof and ferror inspect indicators; clearerr resets them.
Close
fclose(fp) releases the stream and flushes buffered output.

blocks.text: The example shows the complete open → write → close → reopen → read → close sequence. Check each operation; in particular fscanf must make the expected number of conversions and fclose may report a delayed write failure.
